generation.prompt:
Use case: style-transfer
Asset type: Paper Trails circular timeline portrait.
Input images: Image 1 is the sole identity reference, the historical engraved likeness of William Derham. Images 2, 3 and 4 are approved Rutherford, Bohr and Alfvén house-style references only; never borrow their faces.
Primary request: draw a fresh affectionate editorial caricature of William Derham in the Wry Engraver style, recognisable before humorous.
Recognition anchors: broad softly rounded clean-shaven face with pronounced long straight nose; shoulder-length wavy dark hair parted near the centre, receding slightly at the temples; alert level eyes and a quietly pursed mouth. Retain his three-quarter turn towards the viewer's left and the two rectangular white clerical bands above the dark robe.
Comic idea: his generous clerical bands and slightly inquisitive eyebrow are the only understated visual beat. No props or hands.
Style: bold charcoal-teal ink contour, simplified graphic shapes, restrained flat fills, one shallow shadow tone and faint print grain. Match the approved graphic reference portraits, never colourise the engraving.
Composition: centred head-and-shoulders bust. Hair begins 8% from top, shoulders reach bottom edge, eyes near 42% canvas height. Face, hair and clerical bands readable and safely cropped at 42px and 92px circular sizes; important facial features inside central 76%.
Palette: charcoal-teal and muted brown-black period robe and hair, cream clerical bands; natural neutral pink-beige skin. The sepia engraving is an identity source, not a skin colour. No yellow, orange, bronze or sepia cast.
Background: genuine alpha transparency; empty pixels outside the bust; never draw or depict a checkerboard, transparency grid, studio backdrop, halo, or background colour.
Constraints: square 1024×1024 RGBA PNG. Preserve documented facial identity and period clothes. No text, captions, signature, watermark, apparatus or full body. Avoid photorealism, dense engraving hatching, airbrushing and gradients.
